title: Where Should Physics Enter? Information, Identifiability and Calibration in Probabilistic Sea Surface Temperature Forecasting
abstract: arXiv:2611.23129v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Advection-diffusion priors are a common way to make neural sea surface temperature (SST) forecasts physics-informed. We test where such a prior must enter a heteroscedastic ConvLSTM to help, using daily NOAA OISST v2.1 for the Bay of Bengal (1982-2024) and a synthetic benchmark on the same grid with known currents of controlled strength. (i) On real data, a soft advection-diffusion residual with a learned velocity gives no reliable benefit (lead-15 CRPS -0.007 degrees C, 95% interval [-0.022, +0.008]); a plain temporal-smoothness penalty matches it, and equivalence within 3% is not established either. (ii) Learned velocities do not recover the currents, whether placed in the loss, in an explicit transport step, or in a transport step without neural correction: they correlate with the reference no better than a shuffled-date null, even on synthetic data where knowing the currents would improve day-15 forecasts by 16-23%. translated_title: 物理应从何处介入？概率性海表温度预测中的信息、可辨识性与校准
translated_abstract: 平流-扩散先验是使神经网络海表温度（SST）预测具备物理信息的一种常用手段。我们测试了此类先验应在异方差ConvLSTM的哪个环节介入才能真正起到帮助作用，实验使用孟加拉湾（1982-2024年）的每日NOAA OISST v2.1数据，以及在同一网格上构建的、具有已知可控强度洋流的合成基准数据集。(i) 在真实数据上，采用学习速度场的软平流-扩散残差并未带来可靠的收益（提前15天CRPS为-0.007°C，95%置信区间为[-0.022, +0.008]）；一个简单的时序平滑惩罚便可达到同等效果，且二者在3%范围内的等效性也无法确立。(ii) 学习得到的速度场无法恢复真实洋流，无论将其置于损失函数中、显式输运步骤中，还是不含神经校正的输运步骤中：即便在合成数据上——已知洋流可使第15天预测提升16-23%——它们与参考洋流的相关性也不优于打乱日期的零假设。(iii) 提供的洋流（原文此处被截断）
tldr: 该论文系统性地测试了平流-扩散物理先验在神经海表温度预测模型中的不同介入位置，发现学习得到的速度场既无法带来可靠的预测收益，也无法辨识出真实洋流——即使洋流信息理论上可大幅提升预测精度——揭示了物理信息神经网络中可辨识性与校准的关键问题。
en_tdlr: This paper systematically tests where advection-diffusion physics priors should enter neural SST forecasting models, showing that learned velocity fields provide neither reliable forecast benefits nor identifiability of true ocean currents—even when current knowledge could substantially improve predictions—highlighting fundamental issues of information, identifiability and calibration in physics-informed neural networks.
